summary:
Łódź Voivodeship stands within Poland's national legal framework, and the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor in that framework is detention. In a case publicised by the Association for Legal Intervention on 13 March 2024, a regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Her hormone therapy was interrupted for three months because the centre would not supply the medication, and she was released only after NGO intervention prompted the Border Guard commander to order it. The same case documented her history of violence and sexual assault, indicating that trans women held in these facilities may face both untreated care needs and vulnerable placement.

Polish courts and the European Court of Human Rights have proved willing to intervene on that exposure. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages while rejecting the Article 3 claim. The ruling establishes that medication denial in Polish custody is litigable and winnable, though Poland operates no specialised trans prison section and placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry is straightforward for many nationalities. Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days, and lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, linking general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance.

The national legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement. The status of these bills at the time of travel should be verified rather than assumed.

Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal vacuum contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

At regional level, Łódź Voivodeship's own anti-LGBT resolution was revoked by the Supreme Administrative Court of Poland on 12 October 2023. It had been one of five voivodeships, with Lublin, Lesser Poland, Podkarpackie and Świętokrzyskie, written to by the European Commission on 2 June 2020 over such resolutions; the Świętokrzyskie council revoked its own on 22 September 2021. By 24 April 2025 every anti-LGBTQ resolution and every Local Government Family Rights Charter in Poland had been withdrawn or invalidated by court order.

Between 2019 and 2025 more than 100 Polish local governments adopted 'LGBT-free zone'-style resolutions which at their peak covered roughly a third of the country's land area. Administrative courts struck them down as unconstitutional under Article 32 on equal treatment, the European Commission linked EU development funds to their repeal, and the last remaining zone in Łańcut was abolished in 2025. The resolutions were symbolic and institutional rather than criminal: they created no new penalties and barred no one physically, but they signalled to local bureaucracies and schools which families and identities local leadership considered legitimate.
tangentialFactors:
Łódź Voivodeship is not an outlier in the pattern it illustrates. It was one of five voivodeships singled out by the European Commission in its letter of 2 June 2020, and one of more than 100 local governments that adopted such resolutions between 2019 and 2025, at the peak covering roughly a third of Poland's land area. Repeal ran in the opposite direction: Świętokrzyskie withdrew its resolution on 22 September 2021, Łańcut abolished the last remaining zone in 2025, and by 24 April 2025 nothing of this kind survived anywhere in Poland.

The nature of the resolutions matters for expectation-setting. Administrative courts treated them as unconstitutional under Article 32 on equal treatment, and the European Commission tied EU development funds to their repeal, but the instruments themselves created no new offences and imposed no physical restriction on entry or movement. Their effect was signalling to schools and municipal bureaucracies about which identities local leadership regarded as legitimate, so their disappearance removes a formal designation rather than an enforcement measure. The visitor-facing risks that remain documented in Poland are the ones attached to custody and to harassment reported in travel advisories.
localsOnly:
Residents of Łódź Voivodeship lived for several years under a regional resolution of the type the Supreme Administrative Court revoked on 12 October 2023, and the voivodeship's council was among those the European Commission addressed on 2 June 2020. For people living there, the practical significance of the resolution lay in what it told schools and local offices about the standing of same-sex couples and gender-diverse residents, since the text created no penalty and no bar on presence.

Resident-facing protections have widened at national level. The June 2024 revocation of the directive blocking recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad means foreign marriages are no longer refused on that basis, and the September 2024 European Court of Human Rights judgment puts pressure on Poland to create a partnership framework. Hate-speech protection covering gender identity and sexual orientation was announced by Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek, with a March draft Penal Code amendment clearing the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed and a second bill following in late October 2024, alongside a special response team and guidelines issued by the Prosecutor General. Whether each of those instruments is in force is a matter for residents to confirm directly with the authorities concerned.

Trans residents face the custody conditions documented nationally: Poland runs no specialised trans prison section, and placement is decided case by case, which is why the European Court of Human Rights awarded EUR 8,000 on 11 July 2024 over the denial of hormone replacement therapy to a trans prisoner.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the March draft Penal Code amendment and the second hate-speech bill introduced in late October 2024 at the time of travel is unresolved in the available sources; both should be verified against current legislative records rather than assumed to be in force.

Whether any replacement inclusive measure was adopted by the Łódź Voivodeship council after the Supreme Administrative Court revoked its resolution on 12 October 2023 is not sourced here. The inventory establishes that the hostile resolutions are gone nationwide as of 24 April 2025, not that affirmative regional protections followed.

No source in this inventory reports enforcement outcomes, complaint handling or prosecution data for harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity within Łódź Voivodeship, so the practical reliability of the announced protection machinery in this region remains unverified.
